overview: Air New Zealand is the flag-carrier airline of New Zealand, operating an extensive domestic network (20 destinations, ~380 flights/day) alongside international passenger and cargo services across the Pacific Rim - Australia, the Pacific Islands, Asia and North America - supported by alliance partners including United Airlines, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific and Air China. The airline is roughly 51% owned by the New Zealand Government (via the Crown), making it a quasi-strategic national asset as well as a listed equity. Revenue is generated primarily from passenger ticket sales (~87% of FY2025 revenue), supplemented by cargo and a growing Airpoints loyalty/ancillary business.

business_model.summary: Air New Zealand earns revenue by selling passenger seats across domestic, Tasman/Pacific short-haul and long-haul international routes, plus air cargo capacity and ancillary/loyalty income. It is a capital-intensive, operationally-leveraged business: revenue is transactional (ticket-by-ticket) rather than recurring, though the Airpoints loyalty programme (5m+ members) and ancillary fees provide a smaller, stickier revenue stream. Profitability is highly sensitive to fuel prices, FX, capacity/fleet availability and macro-driven travel demand.

revenue_streams.name: Passenger revenue (domestic + international)
revenue_streams.trend: pressured - down 1.5% in FY2025 on capacity constraints and soft domestic demand

revenue_streams.name: Cargo
revenue_streams.trend: growing - up 6% in FY2025 on stronger long-haul load factors

revenue_streams.name: Contract services, other revenue and income (incl. engine compensation)
revenue_streams.trend: volatile - inflated by one-off engine manufacturer compensation receipts

business_model.customer_type: B2C leisure and corporate/government travelers domestically and internationally; B2B cargo and contract/ground-handling services; loyalty ecosystem partners (retail, finance) via Airpoints
business_model.geographic_mix: Domestic New Zealand ~82% market share is the core profit engine; international short-haul (Australia/Pacific) and long-haul (Asia, North America) provide network breadth and connect to global alliance partners; revenue and costs are exposed to NZD/USD and NZD/AUD FX

competitive_position.market_position: Dominant domestic New Zealand carrier with ~82% market share, but this position is now under sustained attack: Jetstar announced its largest-ever New Zealand/Tasman network expansion (2025/26), adding 660,000+ new seats, new domestic routes (e.g., Hamilton-Christchurch), and Jetstar fares typically run 40-50% below Air NZ on comparable routes. Internationally, Air NZ is a mid-sized network carrier reliant on partnerships (Star Alliance-adjacent bilateral deals with United, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Air China) rather than full alliance membership, competing against much larger full-service and low-cost carriers on long-haul legs.

moat_factors.description: ~82% domestic market share and the most comprehensive NZ regional network provide a structural cost and reach advantage that is difficult for new entrants to replicate given NZ's small, geographically dispersed population
~51% Crown ownership provides implicit support (e.g., COVID-era recapitalisation) and slot/route access, but also invites political scrutiny of pricing, service levels and capital decisions
Named World's Safest Airline for 2025 by AirlineRatings.com; strong domestic brand loyalty and Airpoints programme (5m+ members, near-ubiquitous household penetration) support pricing and retention
Baa1 (Moody's) rating, one of the highest-rated airlines globally, gives access to capital at competitive rates versus most global peers - a real advantage in a capital-intensive industry

Partnerships with United, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific and Air China extend reach to 600+ destinations without full alliance capital commitment, though this is weaker than full global alliance membership

weaknesses: Small scale relative to global network carriers limits negotiating leverage with aircraft/engine OEMs, fuel suppliers and lessors
Reliance on a narrow set of long-haul routes and partner airlines for connectivity beyond the Pacific Rim
High fixed-cost base (aircraft ownership/leases, crew, engineering) with limited ability to flex quickly when demand or fuel costs move sharply
Domestic monopoly position now being directly challenged by Jetstar's aggressive capacity expansion and discount pricing

Heavy dependence on two engine manufacturers (Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce) whose global maintenance backlogs have grounded up to 20% of the jet fleet for two consecutive years, a risk largely outside management's control
Government majority ownership can constrain some capital allocation/strategic flexibility (e.g., political sensitivity around fare increases, job cuts)

growth_drivers: Fleet renewal: new GE-powered Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners and Airbus A321neo deliveries improving unit costs and reliability as engine issues resolve
Cabin retrofit programme (Business Premier Luxe seats, new interiors) across the Dreamliner fleet lifting premium yields and customer experience
Domestic network growth (new/reinstated routes such as Hamilton-Christchurch, Christchurch-Adelaide, capacity growth into Wellington/Queenstown)
Airpoints loyalty programme expansion - new partners (Woolworths Everyday Rewards, Sharesies) driving ancillary/non-airline revenue and member engagement (5m+ members)
Digital/AI-driven cost-out and productivity initiatives (Kia Mau strategy targeting ~$100m/year of benefits; automated passenger rebooking; AI tooling for ~3,000 staff)
Recovery of grounded fleet capacity through 2026-2027 as Pratt & Whitney/Rolls-Royce maintenance backlogs clear, unlocking pent-up capacity and productivity gains
Cargo network optimisation and new revenue management tools across international markets
New engineering infrastructure (Hangar 4, Christchurch Engine Centre expansion) supporting long-term maintenance capability and resilience

business.description: Up to 11 aircraft (~20% of the jet fleet) grounded at times in FY2025/H1 FY2026 due to global Pratt & Whitney PW1100 GTF and Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 maintenance backlogs; management does not expect the issue to fully ease until around calendar 2027, with only partial 787 fleet restoration expected by mid/late 2026
Jetstar's largest-ever NZ network expansion (660,000+ new seats, new routes, fares 40-50% below Air NZ) directly threatens the ~82% domestic market share that anchors group profitability
Corporate and government travel demand has weakened materially, compounding capacity constraints and pressuring yields

Long-serving CEO Greg Foran departed October 2025 after guiding the airline through COVID; successor Nikhil Ravishankar (former Chief Digital Officer) is new to the CEO role during an unusually turbulent operating period

financial.description: Middle East conflict escalation (early 2026) drove jet fuel from US$85-90/bbl to a peak of US$160-230/bbl; H2 FY2026 fuel costs are now expected to reach ~NZ$980m versus NZ$740m assumed at the February 2026 interim result, a ~NZ$240m headwind that hedging only partially offsets
Revenue and costs (fuel, aircraft leases/debt, engineering) are USD/AUD-exposed; a weaker NZD raises input costs
Large ongoing fleet capex commitments; net debt/EBITDA target range of 1.5x-2.5x could be breached given the FY2026 loss, pressuring the Baa1 investment-grade rating
Engine manufacturer compensation (NZ$129m FY2025, NZ$55m H1 FY2026) partially offsets grounding costs but timing and quantum remain uncertain and subject to negotiation

regulatory.description: ~51% Crown shareholding creates potential for political/strategic considerations (regional route obligations, fare scrutiny, ESG mandates) to override pure commercial decision-making

regulatory.risk: Rising aviation sector levies and charges
regulatory.description: Management flagged sharp recent increases in aviation levies/charges as a further cost headwind into FY2026

2030 emissions guidance (20-25% net reduction from 2019 baseline) and 10% SAF-by-2030 target require sustained investment; SAF availability and cost remain constraints, and future carbon pricing/ETS changes could add cost

macro.description: Geopolitical shocks (Strait of Hormuz disruption) demonstrated how quickly fuel costs can swing FY earnings from modest profit to a large loss; fuel is Air NZ's largest and least controllable cost
Domestic corporate/government travel and consumer discretionary leisure spend are cyclical and have softened amid a weak NZ economy
Engine and aircraft parts shortages are an industry-wide phenomenon (affecting many GTF/Trent operators globally), meaning resolution timing is largely outside Air NZ's control
Aircraft financing/leasing costs are sensitive to global interest rates; investment-grade rating helps mitigate but does not eliminate this exposure

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global and Asia-Pacific aviation demand has broadly normalised post-COVID, but 2025-2026 has been marked by an industry-wide engine durability crisis (GTF, Trent 1000) grounding aircraft globally, and a sharp, geopolitically-driven jet fuel cost shock in early 2026. NZ domestic aviation is entering a more competitive, lower-fare era as Jetstar scales up.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - airlines are classic capital-intensive cyclicals; earnings swing sharply with fuel prices, FX, and consumer/corporate travel demand, as evidenced by the swing from ~$222m EBT (FY2024) to $189m (FY2025) to an expected $340-390m pre-tax LOSS in FY2026
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - significant fleet financing/lease obligations mean higher rates raise the cost of capital for aircraft acquisition, though the Baa1 investment-grade rating provides relatively favourable access to debt markets
key_input_costs: Jet fuel (largest single cost, highly volatile - recently spiked to US$160-230/bbl from US$85-90/bbl)
Aviation sector levies and airport charges
Foreign exchange (USD-denominated fuel/lease costs vs NZD revenue)

recent_developments.event: FY2025 result: EBT of $189m (down from $222m), NPAT $126m (down 14%); engine availability constraints estimated to have cost ~$165m of EBT; up to 11 aircraft (~20% of jet fleet) grounded at times; $129m compensation received from engine manufacturers
CEO Greg Foran announced departure after ~6 years; Nikhil Ravishankar (Chief Digital Officer) named as successor, effective 20 October 2025
Final FY2025 unimputed dividend of 1.25 cps paid (25 Sept 2025); total FY2025 dividends 2.5 cps; $38m returned via share buyback
Jetstar announced its largest-ever NZ/Tasman network expansion - 660,000+ new annual seats, new domestic routes (e.g. Hamilton-Christchurch from 1 Dec 2025), intensifying domestic competition

H1 FY2026 (six months to 31 Dec 2025) result: pre-tax loss of $59m and net loss after tax of $40m (vs $155m EBT/$106m NPAT pcp); revenue up ~1.2%, costs up ~8%; $55m engine compensation received but $90m of estimated lost earnings from continued groundings; interim dividend of 1.25 cps declared and up to $100m share buy-back approved

Air New Zealand suspended FY2026 earnings guidance, citing 'unprecedented volatility' in jet fuel markets following the Iran-Israel-US conflict and closure risk to the Strait of Hormuz; jet fuel spiked from US$85-90/bbl to US$160-230/bbl over ~10 weeks

Air New Zealand issued updated FY2026 outlook: expects a full-year pre-tax LOSS of NZ$340-390m, versus prior profit expectations; H2 fuel costs now forecast at ~NZ$980m vs NZ$740m assumed in February; announced ~NZ$70m of mitigating fare increases and capacity reductions of 3-5% network-wide, plus identification of up to NZ$100m of annualised cost savings

Management reported all Boeing 787 aircraft expected back in service by late June 2026, with full Airbus neo fleet operational by 2027; framed improving fleet availability as key to strengthening operational resilience amid the ongoing fuel-cost shock

guidance.as_of: May 2026 trading update (post H1 FY2026 result)

items.notes: Reversed from a small full-year profit expectation; driven by a ~NZ$240m H2 fuel cost headwind (fuel now expected at ~NZ$980m in H2 vs NZ$740m assumed at Feb interim result) following the 2026 Middle East-driven jet fuel price shock

items.target: Pre-tax loss of $59m; net loss after tax $40m
items.vs_prior: lowered vs pcp ($155m EBT / $106m NPAT in H1 FY2025)
items.notes: Revenue +1.2%, operating costs +8%; $55m engine compensation received, ~$90m of earnings estimated lost to groundings; ASK roughly flat (+0.3%)
Announced alongside fare increases as part of ~NZ$70m of mitigating actions against the fuel cost shock
Accelerated cost-reduction initiatives begun in late 2025, plus a review of capital expenditure plans

items.target: All Boeing 787s back in service by late June 2026; full Airbus neo fleet by 2027
items.notes: Engine maintenance-related groundings expected to ease materially through 2026 and largely resolve by end of calendar 2027 per FY2025 annual report commentary

guidance.management_commentary: Management (new CEO Nikhil Ravishankar and CFO) has characterised the fuel price shock as 'a material external shock' outside the company's control, distinct from the engine-availability issues that dominated FY2025/H1 FY2026. The airline emphasises that fleet availability improvements (787s returning to service, new deliveries) will not translate immediately into earnings uplift given diseconomies of scale from disrupted operations, but should improve resilience and flexibility into FY2027. The Board reiterated its investment-grade credit rating priority and Capital Management Framework (liquidity target $1.2-1.5bn, net debt/EBITDA 1.5x-2.5x, dividend payout 40-70% of underlying NPAT) even as FY2026 dividends and buybacks face pressure from the deteriorating result.

bull_case: Domestic near-monopoly (~82% market share) and dense NZ network remain a durable structural advantage even as Jetstar expands, given New Zealand's small, dispersed population and high barriers to entry

Engine availability crisis is a transient, industry-wide (not Air NZ-specific) problem expected to substantially resolve through 2026-2027, unlocking pent-up capacity, productivity gains and reduced disruption costs
Government majority ownership (~51%) and Baa1 investment-grade credit rating provide a funding/support backstop unusual among global airlines, reducing solvency risk through severe downturns
Fleet renewal (new 787-9s, A321neos, retrofitted cabins) should structurally lower unit costs and lift premium yields once delivered and fully utilised

Depressed share price (down sharply amid the FY2026 loss guidance) may already discount much of the near-term bad news, offering recovery optionality once fuel prices normalise and the fleet is fully available
bear_case: FY2026 pre-tax loss of NZ$340-390m marks a severe earnings reversal, driven by a fuel cost shock that is inherently unpredictable and could recur or persist longer than currently modelled
Jetstar's aggressive, structurally lower-cost expansion into NZ domestic and Tasman routes threatens to erode Air NZ's core profit engine (domestic market share) over the medium term

Engine-related groundings have now persisted for multiple consecutive years (FY2025 and H1 FY2026), with management's own timelines for full resolution repeatedly extended (2026 to 2027), suggesting execution/visibility risk

Government majority ownership can constrain commercial flexibility (fare-setting, cost-cutting, capital allocation) relative to a purely private competitor, particularly during politically sensitive periods of high fares or job losses

High fixed costs, aggressive fleet capex commitments and a weakening balance sheet (net debt/EBITDA likely rising from FY2025's 1.1x) create risk to the investment-grade rating, dividend and buyback programme if losses persist
